paragraphs: Opinions in Leading Them to Concentrate Political Power

If it is true that men in ages of equality readily take up the idea of a great central power, it cannot be doubted, on the other hand, that their habits and feelings dispose them to accept such a power and back it. A few words will show this, since I have already given most of the reasons. *a People in democratic countries have no superiors, no inferiors and no habitual or necessary partners in what they undertake. They easily turn in on themselves and think of themselves as separate beings. I made this point at some length when I dealt with individualism. As a result, it always takes an effort for such men to pull themselves away from their private affairs and attend to public business. Their natural leaning is to hand that business over to the one visible, lasting representative of the community’s interests, namely the state. They do not merely lack a taste for public business; they frequently lack the time. Private life in democratic periods is so busy, so feverish, so crowded with desires and labors, that each individual has almost no energy or leisure left for public life. I would be the last to claim that these inclinations cannot be overcome, since my main purpose in writing this book has been to fight them. My claim is only that today a hidden force is nourishing them in the human heart, and that unless they are checked they will smother it completely.

I have also had occasion to show that two things make democratic nations dread any violent disturbance: the growing love of well-being and the shifting nature of property. Often the love of public tranquility is the only passion such nations still have, and it grows more active and powerful in them in proportion as every other passion droops and dies. This naturally leads the members of the community to keep handing over further rights to the central power, or giving them up. That power alone seems to have a stake in defending those rights, and to use the same means for them that it uses for itself. In ages of equality, nobody is obliged to help his fellow men, and nobody has any right to expect much support from them. Everyone is therefore independent and powerless at once. These two conditions must never be looked at separately or run together, for they give the citizen of a democratic country quite opposite inclinations. His independence fills him with self-reliance and pride among his equals. His weakness makes him feel, now and then, that he needs help from outside. He cannot hope for it from any of them, since they are all powerless and unsympathetic. In this plight he naturally looks to the imposing power that alone stands above the general level of depression. His needs, and above all his desires, keep calling that power to his mind, until in the end he sees it as the only support his weakness can have, and a necessary one. *b This may go further toward explaining a common sight in democratic countries. The very men who cannot bear superiors will put up patiently with a master, and so show their pride and their servility together.

[Footnote b: In democratic communities only the central power has a stable position or lasting undertakings. Every other member of society is in ceaseless stir and change. Now, all governments by nature seek constantly to widen the range of their action. Such a government can hardly fail to succeed in the end, because it acts on a fixed principle and with a constant will, upon men whose position, ideas and desires keep shifting. Members of the community often strengthen the influence of the central power without meaning to. Democratic ages are periods of experiment, innovation and adventure. At such times a multitude of men are always engaged in difficult or novel enterprises, which they pursue alone, with no concern for their fellow men. They may be willing to grant, as a general principle, that the public authority should not interfere in private concerns. Yet each of them makes an exception for the particular concern he is working on. He asks for the authority’s help there and tries to use the government’s influence for his own advantage, while wanting to restrict it everywhere else. Suppose a large number of men make this same exception for a great variety of different purposes. The sphere of the central power then grows imperceptibly in every direction, although each of them wishes it to stay limited. A democratic government thus increases its power merely by lasting. Time is on its side, every incident helps it, and the passions of individuals unconsciously advance it. It may be asserted that the older a democratic community is, the more centralized its government will become.]

The more privileges dwindle and shrink, the more men hate them. Democratic passions would therefore seem to burn hottest just when they have the least fuel. I have already explained why. Where all conditions are unequal, no inequality is large enough to offend the eye. In the midst of general uniformity, though, the slightest difference is hateful, and the more complete the uniformity, the harder that difference is to bear. It is natural, then, that the love of equality should keep growing along with equality itself, and should swell on what it feeds on. This undying hatred, forever kindled anew, sets a democratic people against even the smallest privilege. It is especially favorable to a gradual concentration of all political rights in the hands of the state’s representative alone. The sovereign stands necessarily and unquestionably above every citizen, so he arouses no envy. Each citizen imagines that he is taking from his equals the prerogative he grants to the crown. A man of a democratic age very much dislikes obeying a neighbor who is his equal. He will not admit that such a person has greater ability than he does. He distrusts his fairness and resents his power; he fears him and holds him in contempt; and he loves to remind him, again and again, that both of them depend on the same master. Any central power that follows its natural tendencies courts and encourages the principle of equality, because equality remarkably eases, widens and secures the influence of a central power.

The same can be said of uniformity: every central government worships it. Uniformity spares the government an investigation into an endless number of small details. Those details would demand attention if rules had to be fitted to men, and men were not simply made subject to rules without distinction. So the government likes what the citizens like and naturally hates what they hate. In democratic nations, these shared feelings keep joining the sovereign and every member of the community in a single conviction, and they create a secret and lasting sympathy between them. The government’s faults are forgiven for the sake of its tastes. Public confidence is withdrawn only reluctantly, even amid its excesses and mistakes, and it comes back at the first call. Democratic nations often hate the people who hold the central power, but they always love the power itself.

I have thus arrived at one conclusion by two separate paths. I showed that the principle of equality puts into men’s heads the idea of a single, uniform and strong government. I have now shown that the same principle gives them a taste for it. The nations of our age are therefore moving toward governments of this kind. Their natural bent of mind and heart pulls them that way, and all they need to do to get there is not to restrain themselves along the road. In the democratic ages now opening before us, I believe that individual independence and local liberties will always be products of artificial contrivance, while centralization will be the natural form of government. *c
